15.01.title: The design process and decision matrices
15.01.html:
Machine design is not one calculation. It is a loop: define the need, generate several concepts, select one, analyse it in detail, test, and go round again when something fails. Phase 15 is about the analysis tools for the machine elements every product is built from: shafts, bearings, gears, bolts, springs. Before any of that, though, someone has to pick the concept, and that choice is usually made with a weighted decision matrix.

The weighted decision matrix

List the criteria that matter, give each an importance weight wj​, and score every concept i against every criterion on the same scale (here 1 = poor to 5 = excellent). Normalise the weights so they sum to one, then

Ti​=j∑​w^j​sij​,w^j​=∑k​wk​wj​​.

The concept with the highest total wins. Two properties make this useful and also show its limits:

  1. Only the ratios of the weights matter. Multiplying every weight by 7 changes nothing, because of the normalisation.
  2. Totals are linear in the weights. If you raise one weight w^j​ from 0 to 1 while scaling the others down in proportion, each total moves along a straight line, so the point where two concepts swap is a single linear equation. That is a sensitivity check: if a small change in a weight flips the winner, the matrix has not really decided anything.

The scores are judgements, not measurements. The matrix makes those judgements explicit and easy to argue about, which is its real value.

Worked exampleChoosing a drivetrain for a commuter bike

Four concepts are scored on cost, mass, efficiency, maintenance and gear range:

Concept Cost Mass Efficiency Maintenance Gear range
1x derailleur 4 5 5 2 4
8-speed hub 3 2 3 4 3
belt + hub 1 2 3 5 3
single speed 5 5 5 4 1

A commuter in a wet, flat city gives importance points 25, 20, 15, 30, 10 (out of 100), so the weights are 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.30, 0.10.

  1. Single speed: 0.25⋅5+0.20⋅5+0.15⋅5+0.30⋅4+0.10⋅1=4.30.
  2. 1x derailleur 3.75, 8-speed hub 3.10, belt + hub 2.90. Single speed wins.
  3. Sensitivity: move to a hilly town and raise the gear-range weight λ, scaling the other four in proportion. With λ=0 the totals are 4.667 (single speed) and 3.722 (derailleur); with λ=1 they are 1 and 4. They cross where 0.944=3.944λ, so λ=17/71=0.2394. Above about 24% weight on gear range, the derailleur wins.

Exercise 1Doubling the cost weight

Keep the bike scores. Give cost 50 points and mass, efficiency, maintenance and gear range 20, 10, 10 and 10. What are the new totals for the single speed and the belt + hub, and does the winner change?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Weights: 50, 20, 10, 10, 10 out of 100, so 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1.
  2. Single speed: 0.5⋅5+0.2⋅5+0.1⋅5+0.1⋅4+0.1⋅1=4.50.
  3. Belt + hub: 0.5⋅1+0.2⋅2+0.1⋅3+0.1⋅5+0.1⋅3=2.00.
  4. The 1x derailleur gets 2+1+0.5+0.2+0.4=4.10. Single speed still wins, by a wider margin.

quiz.q: Weighted total of the 8-speed hub with weights 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.30, 0.10. 2 decimals.
Raw importance points 3, 1 and 1. What is the normalised weight of the first criterion?
quiz.explain: Divide by the sum of the points.

quiz.q: Gear-range weight at which the 1x derailleur overtakes the single speed in the example. 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: Totals are linear in the weight: 0.944 = 3.944 λ.

quiz.explain: The weights are normalised, so only ratios count.

quiz.explain: The decision is sensitive; look harder at the criteria or the scores.

15.02.title: Safety factors and reliability
15.02.html:
A safety factor is the ratio of strength to stress, n=R/S. Codes give values such as 1.5 or 2, and for a part with well-known loads and material that is fine. But strength and stress are both scattered: one batch of aluminium is stronger than the next, and one rider hits a pothole harder than another. Two designs with the same safety factor can have very different chances of failing. Stress-strength interference puts a number on that chance.

Two overlapping distributions

Model strength R and stress S as independent normal variables with means μR​,μS​ and standard deviations σR​,σS​. The part fails when R<S, that is when the margin M=R−S is negative. A difference of independent normals is normal, with

μM​=μR​−μS​,σM​=σR2​+σS2​​.

So the probability of failure is

Pf​=P(M<0)=Φ(−z),z=σR2​+σS2​​μR​−μS​​,

where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution and z is the reliability index. The central safety factor μR​/μS​ does not appear on its own: scatter matters as much as the mean margin.

Monte Carlo checks this without any formula: draw a few million (R,S) pairs and count how often R<S. The count has a binomial standard error Pf​(1−Pf​)/N​, and the estimate should land within a few of those of Φ(−z).

Assumptions: normal distributions, independence, and a single failure mode. Real strength data has a lower tail that is often thinner than normal (materials are proof-tested), and loads often have a fatter one, so for very small Pf​ the tails matter more than the formula suggests.

Worked exampleAn aluminium handlebar clamp

Strength 300 MPa with 8% scatter (σR​=24 MPa); peak stress in use 180 MPa with 15% scatter (σS​=27 MPa).

  1. Central safety factor 300/180=1.667.
  2. z=120/242+272​=120/36.12=3.3218, so Pf​=Φ(−3.3218)=4.47×10−4: about 1 clamp in 2240.
  3. Two million Monte Carlo pairs give 4.68×10−4±0.15×10−4, within 1.4 standard errors.
  4. Double both scatters, keep the means: the safety factor is still 1.667, but z=1.661 and Pf​=0.0484, about 1 in 21.
  5. For Pf​=10−6 we need z=4.7534. With strength scatter fixed at 8% of its mean, the mean strength must be 370.6 MPa, a safety factor of 2.06.

Exercise 1A heavier rider

In the clamp example the mean stress rises to 200 MPa, everything else unchanged. Find z and Pf​.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. z=(300−200)/36.12=2.768.
  2. Pf​=Φ(−2.768)=2.82×10−3, about 1 in 355.
  3. An 11% rise in load raised the failure probability more than sixfold. That steep tail is why reliability targets need margin.

quiz.q: Reliability index z for μ_R = 300, σ_R = 24, μ_S = 200, σ_S = 27 (MPa). 3 decimals.
Standard deviation (MPa) of the margin R − S when σ_R = 30 and σ_S = 40.
Failure probability for z = 3. Give it ×10⁻³ with 3 decimals.
Two designs have the same central safety factor. The one with more scatter has:
quiz.explain: A larger σ_M means a smaller z.

15.03.title: Tolerances, fits and stack-ups
15.03.html:
No part is made exactly to size. A drawing that says “25 mm” really means “25 mm give or take something”, and the designer chooses that something. Choose it too tight and the part is expensive; too loose and the bearing rattles or the gear will not press on. This lesson covers the two everyday tools: ISO fits for a shaft in a hole, and stack-up analysis for a chain of parts.

ISO 286 fits

The tolerance grade IT sets the width of the band. ISO 286 builds it from a tolerance unit that grows slowly with size D (the geometric mean of a size step, in mm):

i=0.45D1/3+0.001D  μm,IT6=10i,  IT7=16i,  IT8=25i.

A letter sets the position of the band. In the common basic-hole system the hole is always H (lower deviation zero) and the shaft letter does the work: g sits below zero (clearance), h touches zero, k and n sit above zero (transition), p and s higher still (interference). The fundamental deviations also come from formulas, for example es​=−2.5D0.34 for g, ei​=0.6D1/3 for k and ei​=5D0.34 for n (μm), rounded to whole micrometres.

A fit is then described by its extreme clearances:

cmax​=holemax​−shaftmin​,cmin​=holemin​−shaftmax​.

Both positive: a clearance fit. Both negative: an interference fit. One of each: a transition fit, which may go together loose or tight.

Stack-ups: worst case and root-sum-square

When parts sit end to end, their tolerances add. If a gap is g=∑k​sk​Lk​ with signs sk​=±1 and part tolerances ±tk​:

tWC​=k∑​tk​,tRSS​=∑k​tk2​​≤tWC​.

Worst case guarantees assembly even if every part is at its limit in the bad direction. Root-sum-square assumes the errors are independent and each tolerance is 3σ of a normal distribution; then the gap’s standard deviation is tRSS​/3 and 99.73% of assemblies land inside ±tRSS​. With many parts, RSS is much narrower, because it is unlikely that all parts are off in the same direction at once.

Worked exampleA 25 mm bearing seat and a bike hub stack

  1. For 25 mm the size step is 18 to 30 mm, so D=18⋅30​=23.24 and i=1.308 μm. IT6 = 13 μm and IT7 = 21 μm, the table values.
  2. 25 H7/g6: hole 0 to +21 μm; shaft es​=−2.5⋅23.240.34=−7, so −7 to −20 μm. Clearance from +7 to +41 μm: a sliding fit.
  3. 25 H7/k6: shaft +2 to +15 μm, so from 15 μm interference to 19 μm clearance: a transition fit, typical for a bearing inner ring that must be located but still removable.
  4. A hub stack: housing 50.30 ± 0.10 mm minus two bearings 15.00 ± 0.05 and a spacer 20.00 ± 0.08. Nominal play 0.30 mm. Worst case ± 0.280 mm; RSS 0.12+0.052+0.082+0.052​=±0.146 mm.
  5. A million Monte Carlo assemblies (each tolerance = 3σ) give a play standard deviation of 0.0487 mm, equal to RSS/3, and 0.27% outside the RSS band, as predicted.

Exercise 1A 50 mm shaft

For a 50 mm diameter (size step 30 to 50 mm), compute IT7 and the g6 shaft limits, and the clearance range of 50 H7/g6.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. D=30⋅50​=38.73, i=0.45⋅38.731/3+0.0387=1.561 μm.
  2. IT7 = 16i=25 μm; IT6 = 10i=16 μm.
  3. g: es​=−2.5⋅38.730.34=−8.66→−9 μm, so the shaft is −9 to −25 μm.
  4. Clearance from 0−(−9)=9 μm to 25−(−25)=50 μm.

RSS tolerance (mm) of the same five-part stack. 5 decimals.
Maximum clearance (μm) of a fit with hole 0 to +21 and shaft −7 to −20.

15.04.title: Shaft design for fatigue
15.04.html:
A rotating shaft carrying a gear sees its bending stress go from tension to compression once per revolution, millions of times. So a shaft is almost always designed for fatigue, not for a single static load. The standard recipe combines the bending moment diagram, stress concentration, the Marin endurance limit and the Goodman line into one diameter formula.

Loads on a rotating shaft

For a shaft supported in two bearings with point loads, statics gives the reactions and the bending moment M(x), which peaks under a load. Because the shaft rotates while the load direction stays fixed in space, a fibre on the surface sees fully reversed bending: alternating moment Ma​=M, mean Mm​=0. The torque from the gear is usually steady: Tm​=T, Ta​=0.

The DE-Goodman diameter

Combine bending and torsion with the distortion-energy (von Mises) equivalent stress, apply the fatigue stress concentration factors Kf​ (bending) and Kfs​ (torsion) at the shoulder, and put the alternating and mean parts on the Goodman line σa′​/Se​+σm′​/Sut​=1/n. Solving for d:

d=[π16n​(Se​4(Kf​Ma​)2+3(Kfs​Ta​)2​​+Sut​4(Kf​Mm​)2+3(Kfs​Tm​)2​​)]1/3.

The endurance limit itself depends on the diameter through the size factor kb​=1.24d−0.107 (for 2.8 to 51 mm), with Se​=ka​kb​0.5Sut​ and the machined-surface factor ka​=4.51Sut−0.265​. So the formula is solved by fixed-point iteration: guess d, compute Se​, compute a new d, repeat. It converges in a handful of steps because kb​ varies slowly.

Assumptions: steady torque, fully reversed bending, a single critical section, Goodman (slightly conservative compared with test data), and Kf​ values taken as given. In a real design you check every shoulder and keyway, and the deflection and critical speed too.

Worked exampleA gearbox countershaft

Bearings 300 mm apart; a gear force of 2000 N at 100 mm and a pulley pull of 1200 N at 220 mm, both in the same plane. Steady torque 150 N·m. 1045 cold-drawn steel, Sut​=630 MPa; shoulder Kf​=1.7, Kfs​=1.5; target n=2.

  1. Reactions: R2​=(2000⋅100+1200⋅220)/300=1546.7 N, R1​=1653.3 N.
  2. Peak moment under the gear: M=1653.3⋅0.1=165.33 N·m (at the pulley it is 1546.7⋅0.08=123.7 N·m).
  3. ka​=4.51⋅630−0.265=0.817. After iterating, d=31.84 mm, kb​=0.856, Se​=220.4 MPa.
  4. Bending term 2⋅1.7⋅165333/220.4=2550.2; torsion term 3​⋅1.5⋅150000/630=618.6. Then d=[10.186⋅3168.8]1/3=31.84 mm.
  5. Back-check: σa′​=88.70 MPa, σm′​=61.49 MPa, and 1/(88.70/220.4+61.49/630)=2.000.
  6. For n = 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 the diameter is 28.85, 31.84, 34.37, 36.59 mm: a larger safety factor always needs a larger shaft, roughly as n1/3. A designer would pick the next standard size, 32 or 35 mm.

Exercise 1Without the torque

If the same shaft carried the bending loads but no torque, what diameter would n=2 need? And with 50% more bending moment and the torque back?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. With T=0 only the bending term remains; iterating gives d=29.54 mm.
  2. With M=248.0 N·m and T=150 N·m, d=35.77 mm.
  3. The bending term dominates: dropping all the torque saves only 2.3 mm, while 50% more bending adds 3.9 mm.

quiz.q: Peak bending moment (N·m) of a 400 mm simply supported shaft with 3000 N at 150 mm. 2 decimals.
Size factor k_b for a 30 mm shaft. 4 decimals.
Doubling n multiplies the diameter by about (ignore the change in k_b). 3 decimals.
For a rotating shaft with a fixed-direction load, the bending stress is:
quiz.explain: Each fibre passes the tension and compression sides every revolution.

15.05.title: Keys, splines and press fits
15.05.html:
A gear on a shaft has to pass torque without slipping. There are three classic ways: a key in a slot, a spline (many keys machined into the shaft), or a press fit, where the hub bore is made slightly smaller than the shaft and friction does the work. The press fit has no slot to weaken the shaft, but its capacity depends entirely on the contact pressure, and that comes from thick-cylinder elasticity.

Keys and splines

A parallel key of width w, height h and length L on a shaft of diameter d carries the force F=2T/d at the shaft surface. Two checks:

τ=dwL2T​  (shear across the key),σc​=dhL4T​  (crushing on half the key height).

For a square key (w=h) the crushing stress is twice the shear stress. The key is meant to be the weak link: it is cheap to replace, and it protects the shaft and hub. A spline spreads the same torque over many teeth, so it is shorter for the same torque and lets a hub slide axially, as on a gearbox selector or a bike’s freehub body.

Press fits from Lamé

A hub (bore R, outer radius ro​) is forced onto a solid shaft of radius R+δ, where δ is the radial interference. Both parts are thick cylinders. Lamé's solution gives the radial displacement of each under the interface pressure p; the hub bore must grow and the shaft shrink by a total of δ:

δ=pR[Eo​1​(ro2​−R2ro2​+R2​+νo​)+Ei​1​(1−νi​)].

For the same material on both sides this simplifies to

p=2Rro2​Eδ(ro2​−R2)​.

Friction then gives the torque and axial capacity, and the hub bore carries the largest hoop stress:

T=2πR2Lμp,Faxial​=2πRLμp,σt,bore​=pro2​−R2ro2​+R2​.

Assumptions: plane stress, both parts elastic, hub length equal to the fit length, and a friction coefficient around 0.1 to 0.2 for dry steel (it varies a lot, so press fits are rated conservatively). The code checks Lamé against an independent finite-difference solution of the radial displacement equation u′′+u′/r−u/r2=0.

Worked exampleA scooter gear pressed on a 20 mm shaft

Steel hub, outer diameter 60 mm, length 25 mm, on a 20 mm steel shaft; diametral interference 20 μm (radial δ=0.010 mm); E=207 GPa, μ=0.15.

  1. p=207000⋅0.010⋅(900−100)/(2⋅10⋅900)=92.0 MPa. The finite-difference solution agrees to better than 0.01%.
  2. Torque capacity T=2π⋅102⋅25⋅0.15⋅92.0=216.8 N·m; push-out force 21.68 kN.
  3. Hoop stress at the hub bore: 92.0⋅1000/800=115.0 MPa, comfortably elastic for steel.
  4. A 6 × 6 mm key, 25 mm long, carrying 100 N·m instead: shear 2⋅100000/(20⋅6⋅25)=66.7 MPa, crushing 133.3 MPa.

Exercise 1Using a standard fit

The same hub uses a 20 H7/s6 fit. From the ISO tables, the hole is 0 to +21 μm and the s6 shaft is +35 to +48 μm. Find the range of contact pressure and torque capacity, and the largest hub hoop stress.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Diametral interference from 35−21=14 μm to 48−0=48 μm, so radial 7 to 24 μm.
  2. p=207000⋅800/18000⋅δ=9200δ: from 64.4 to 220.8 MPa.
  3. Torque from 151.7 N·m (loosest) to 520.2 N·m (tightest). Design on the loosest: 151.7 N·m.
  4. Largest hoop stress 220.8⋅1.25=276.0 MPa, still below the yield strength of a medium-carbon steel hub, but worth checking.

15.06.title: Rolling bearings and fatigue life
15.06.html:
A ball bearing does not wear out like a brake pad. If it is clean and lubricated, it fails by rolling contact fatigue: after many millions of stress cycles, a crack starts below the surface of a race and a flake of metal spalls out. The time to that event is random, even for identical bearings under identical loads, so bearing life is a statistical quantity.

The L10 life

The basic rating life L10​ is the number of revolutions that 90% of a large group of identical bearings survive. Tests show it follows a power law in the load:

L10​=(PC​)a million revolutions,a=3 (ball),a=310​ (roller).

C is the dynamic load rating from the catalogue: the load giving L10​ = one million revolutions. P is the equivalent load. For combined radial and axial load the catalogue gives P=XFr​+YFa​, with X and Y depending on the ratio Fa​/Fr​ and the bearing type. Because of the cube law, doubling the load cuts a ball bearing’s life by 8, and a 10% overload costs about 25% of the life.

Rearranged for selection: Creq​=PL1/a, with L in millions of revolutions.

Other reliabilities

Fatigue lives scatter roughly as a Weibull distribution: the fraction surviving to life L is exp[−(L/η)b], with slope b≈1.5 for ball bearings. Anchoring it at the L10​ point gives the life at any reliability R:

LR​=L10​(ln(1/0.9)ln(1/R)​)1/b.

So 95% reliability gives 0.62L10​, 99% gives 0.21L10​, and the median bearing lasts 3.5L10​. (ISO 281 tabulates slightly different factors, 0.64 and 0.25, because it adds a minimum life below which no bearing fails.)

Worked exampleA scooter wheel bearing

A 6202 deep groove ball bearing has C=8060 N. On a scooter wheel of 450 mm diameter it carries an equivalent load of 1500 N (weight plus a dynamic allowance).

  1. L10​=(8060/1500)3=155.1 million revolutions. The wheel rolls 1.414 m per revolution, so that is about 219 000 km.
  2. At 3000 N: 155.1/8=19.4 million revolutions.
  3. Combined load Fr​=1200 N, Fa​=400 N with catalogue factors X=0.56, Y=1.8: P=672+720=1392 N, L10​=194.1 million revolutions.
  4. At 95% reliability the life is 0.619L10​=96.0 million revolutions.
  5. A simulated fleet of 200 000 bearings with Weibull lives: 10.01% fail before L10​, and the median is 3.51L10​, as the formula says.

The fatigue life is huge, yet scooter wheel bearings in Bali often last only a few years. Real bearings in wet, sandy service fail from contamination and corrosion long before fatigue; the catalogue’s life modification factors (ISO 281 aISO​) can cut the life tenfold or more for dirty conditions. Seals matter more than C here.

Exercise 1Choosing a bearing

A gearbox shaft runs at 1500 rpm with an equivalent radial load of 2.2 kN, and must reach 20 000 hours with 90% reliability. What dynamic rating is needed for a ball bearing and for a roller bearing?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Revolutions: 1500⋅60⋅20000=1.8×109=1800 million.
  2. Ball: C=2200⋅18001/3=2200⋅12.164=26760 N, so about 26.8 kN (a 6306 has 33.2 kN, enough).
  3. Roller: C=2200⋅18000.3=2200⋅9.475=20850 N, about 20.8 kN.

quiz.q: L10 (million revolutions) for a ball bearing with C = 12 kN at P = 2 kN.
